title: Bounding Freedom Of Choice Via Causal Network Embeddings
authors: George Moreno, Emanuele Polino, Giovanni Rodari, Davide Poderini, Askery Canabarro, Elie Wolfe, Robert W. Spekkens, Fabio Sciarrino, Rafael Chaves
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard Bell inequalities rely on measurement independence, the assumption that measurement settings are perfectly decoupled from the source of correlations. We demonstrate that embedding Bell scenarios into larger causal networks naturally overcomes this limitation. This embedding yields experimentally accessible lower and upper bounds on measurement dependence, the incompatibility of which certifies nonclassicality directly from data, without assuming a priori freedom of choice. We formulate a general linear-programming framework to systematically derive these measurement-dependence consistency (MDC) Bell inequalities. By bypassing standard non-convexity hurdles, this approach significantly outperforms existing techniques in computational simplicity and noise robustness. Finally, we reveal that genuine quantum nonlocality can be certified even for correlations exceeding the Tsirelson bound, and demonstrate our method's broad applicability to multi-outcome and multipartite Bell tests.
tldr: The paper introduces causal-network embeddings of Bell scenarios to derive measurement-dependence consistency inequalities that certify nonclassicality without assuming freedom of choice.
motivation: Standard Bell tests assume measurement independence, an assumption that can be violated in realistic experiments and undermines device-independent certification; the authors aim to remove this assumption by bounding measurement dependence directly from observed data.
method: They embed Bell scenarios into larger causal networks and formulate a general linear-programming framework to systematically derive measurement-dependence consistency Bell inequalities, avoiding non-convexity issues and enabling noise-robust experimental tests.
result: The framework yields experimentally accessible lower and upper bounds on measurement dependence whose incompatibility certifies nonclassicality, outperforms existing techniques computationally, and shows genuine quantum nonlocality can be certified even for correlations exceeding the Tsirelson bound, with applicability to multi-outcome and multipartite Bell tests.
conclusion: Causal network embeddings provide a practical and general route to Bell-type certification without a priori freedom of choice, broadening the scope of nonlocality tests and measurement-dependence analysis.

title: Device-independent Witnesses Of Genuine Multipartite Entanglement And Nonlocality For Ghz States And Bell-pair Tree
authors: Josep Batle, Tomasz Bia{\l}ecki, Adam Bednorz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive and compare device-independent witnesses of genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) and genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL) for GHZ states and trees of Bell pairs. A binary-outcome family using four global measurement contexts has the tight biseparable bound independent of the number of parties. We distinguish these GME bounds from Svetlichny-hybrid bounds, which permit arbitrary communication within either side of a bipartition. For GHZ states, we also give a [MATH]-context GMNL witness and compare it with MABK and Svetlichny tests. For Bell-pair trees, sums of CHSH and chained inequalities certify GME and GMNL, respectively, with explicitly specified input protocols and multi-bit local outputs. Separately, we prove the sharp four-context network bound [MATH] for every [MATH] and [MATH], and bound the MABK scores of quantum networks assembled from bipartite sources. We successfully benchmark MABK, four-context, and Svetlichny witnesses on IBM Quantum GHZ preparations up to [MATH] parties, under the local-measurement and sampling assumptions.
tldr: The paper derives and benchmarks device-independent witnesses for genuine multipartite entanglement and nonlocality in GHZ states and Bell-pair trees, including tight bounds and IBM Quantum tests.
motivation: Genuine multipartite entanglement and nonlocality are central resources for device-independent quantum information protocols, but practical witnesses with strong bounds and experimental viability are needed.
method: The authors construct binary-outcome witnesses using four global measurement contexts, compare them with Svetlichny, MABK, CHSH, and chained inequalities, and prove network bounds for multipartite scenarios.
result: They obtain a tight biseparable bound independent of party number, give a four-context GMNL witness for GHZ states, certify GME/GMNL for Bell-pair trees via CHSH/chained sums, and benchmark witnesses on IBM Quantum GHZ states up to several parties.
conclusion: The proposed witnesses provide useful device-independent tools for certifying genuine multipartite entanglement and nonlocality, with experimental demonstrations supporting their applicability.

They distinguish these GME bounds from Svetlichny-hybrid bounds, which allow arbitrary communication within either side of a bipartition. For GHZ states, they also provide a 2N-context GMNL witness and compare it with MABK and Svetlichny tests. title: Optimal Driving Between Nonequilibrium Steady States Under A Dissipation Budget
authors: Keisuke Sugie, Dimitri Loutchko, Tetsuya J. Kobayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driving between nonequilibrium steady states incurs two thermodynamic costs: excess entropy production (EP) resulting from changing control parameters, and housekeeping EP required to sustain steady currents. Conventional fixed-duration optimization minimizes the former while neglecting the latter. Here, we instead optimize excess EP over both the protocol and its duration subject to a fixed leading order of housekeeping-EP budget, thereby minimizing total EP for that budget constraint. In the slow-driving regime, accumulated housekeeping EP acts as an entropic time, mapping the problem to a geodesic optimization under a friction metric weighted by the steady-state EP rate. This resource-based geometry determines optimal paths and schedules for systems that continue to dissipate even in steady states, establishing an intrinsic trade-off between housekeeping and excess EPs. Near equilibrium, this framework further yields geometric lower bounds on total EP, attained with equipartition at the optimal budget given by a modified thermodynamic length. Numerical simulations of a three-state model for an ATP-driven calcium pump reveal distinct optimal protocols compared to fixed-duration driving, confirming the total-EP bounds.
tldr: The paper optimizes driving protocols between nonequilibrium steady states by jointly minimizing excess and housekeeping entropy production under a fixed housekeeping-EP budget, yielding a resource-based thermodynamic geometry for optimal paths and schedules.
motivation: Conventional fixed-duration optimization neglects the housekeeping entropy production needed to sustain nonequilibrium steady currents, so total thermodynamic cost is not properly minimized.
method: In the slow-driving regime, accumulated housekeeping entropy production is treated as an entropic time, mapping the problem to geodesic optimization under a friction metric weighted by the steady-state entropy production rate.
result: The framework determines optimal paths and schedules under the budget constraint, establishes an intrinsic trade-off between housekeeping and excess entropy production, and yields geometric lower bounds on total entropy production near equilibrium, verified numerically with a three-state ATP-driven calcium pump model.
conclusion: Accounting for housekeeping costs qualitatively changes optimal driving between nonequilibrium steady states and provides a geometric thermodynamic framework for systems that continue to dissipate even in steady operation.

title: The Memory Cost Of Sequential Quantum State Preparation
authors: Patryk Lipka-Bartosik Jian Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much memory does a quantum device need to prepare systems one at a time? We address this question through the lens of quantum resource theories, which formalize physical restrictions on how the memory may interact with the stream of systems it processes. By comparing sequential with collective preparation, we show that under general assumptions both have the same asymptotic memory cost per output. Still, sequential preparation can require an unboundedly larger memory than collective one, and we investigate how this gap depends on the physical restrictions on the allowed interactions. For energy-conserving unitaries, we determine both optimal memory dimensions needed for preparing pure states from an energy eigenstate, and find that the extra memory required sequentially either remains bounded or grows logarithmically with the number of outputs. Under noisy operations, we reveal transformations for which one auxiliary qubit suffices for preparing arbitrarily many independent outputs collectively, while no memory of fixed dimension can deliver them sequentially. Finally, for sequential protocols that repeat a fixed interaction, we show that a [MATH]-dimensional memory that succeeds for [MATH] rounds will succeed forever, and that such a sequential preparation is equivalent to quantum catalysis.
tldr: The paper analyzes the memory cost of preparing quantum states sequentially versus collectively using quantum resource theories, showing equal asymptotic per-output memory but potentially unbounded sequential overhead depending on allowed interactions.
motivation: Quantum devices often prepare systems one at a time, raising the question of how much memory is required under physical restrictions on memory-system interactions.
method: The authors compare sequential and collective preparation within quantum resource theories, focusing on energy-conserving unitaries, noisy operations, and repeated fixed interactions.
result: They find the same asymptotic memory cost per output, but sequential preparation can require unboundedly more memory; under energy conservation the overhead is bounded or logarithmic, while under noisy operations one auxiliary qubit can suffice collectively but no fixed-dimensional memory works sequentially.
conclusion: Sequential state preparation faces resource-theoretic memory limitations, and repeated-interaction sequential protocols are shown to be equivalent to quantum catalysis.

Finally, for sequential protocols repeating a fixed interaction, they prove that a d-dimensional memory succeeding for d^2 rounds will succeed forever, and that such sequential preparation is equivalent to quantum catalysis.

title: Quantum Telatar Formula: Fading Quantum Capacity Of Haar-random Multimode Attenuators
authors: Victor V. Albert Eric Culf
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cellular communication is done over an imperfectly predictable multimode environment, where the sender only knows about the distribution of possible intermode coupling and scattering a signal faces. It may thus seem surprising that such communication is efficient. Telatar proved that the sender's lack of exact knowledge about the channel, on average, does not significantly hinder multimode communication. As the number [MATH] of modes increases at fixed signal-to-noise ratio, the average capacity of a classical multimode fading channel grows linearly in [MATH], like that of [MATH] decoupled single-mode channels. We study the quantum analogue in a Haar-random passive bosonic network and prove a similar scaling for unassisted quantum information transmission. Suppose that the sender drives a fixed fraction of the input modes and the receiver collects more than half of the output modes. Then the quantum capacity of such channels at zero temperature grows linearly with the number of modes at fixed photon number per mode, just like the classical capacity grows with the number of antennas. At nonzero temperature, the Haar-averaged coherent information of the isotropic thermal input bounds the capacity from below, and its value per mode converges to an integral against Wachter's law. We numerically identify positive achievable rates in models motivated by cryogenic microwave networks and room-temperature multimode fibers.
tldr: The paper establishes a quantum analogue of Telatar's classical fading-channel capacity result for Haar-random multimode bosonic attenuators, showing linear scaling of unassisted quantum capacity with mode number under fixed photon number per mode.
motivation: Classical multimode fading channels are known to achieve linear capacity scaling despite sender ignorance of the exact channel realization, but the quantum analogue for bosonic networks was not established.
method: The authors analyze Haar-random passive bosonic networks, prove scaling of quantum capacity when a fixed fraction of input modes is driven and more than half of output modes are collected, and bound capacity from below at nonzero temperature using the Haar-averaged coherent information of isotropic thermal inputs.
result: At zero temperature the quantum capacity grows linearly with the number of modes at fixed photon number per mode, and at nonzero temperature the per-mode coherent-information lower bound converges to an integral against Wachter's law; positive achievable rates are numerically identified in cryogenic microwave and room-temperature fiber-inspired models.
conclusion: The work extends Telatar-type fading capacity scaling to quantum information transmission through random multimode attenuators, providing both asymptotic results and numerically achievable rates for realistic bosonic network models.

Numerical results identify positive achievable rates in models inspired by cryogenic microwave networks and room-temperature multimode fibers, demonstrating practical relevance.

title: Css Circuits: Useful Quantum Circuits That Can Be Simulated With $o(1)$ Cost Per Gate

abstract: ArXiv:2611.14944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: "CSS circuits" are quantum circuits generated by [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and CNOT gates. title: Time- And Photon-Optimal Paths For The Preparation And Logical Flip Of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill States
authors: Aidan Curtis, Juan S. Salcedo-Gallo, Sergei Leonov, Kevin Limanta, Peter Chin, Salil Bedkihal, Mattias Fitzpatrick
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are highly non-Gaussian, making their control challenging, particularly in the presence of photon loss. Here, we use the brachistochrone, the fastest path at bounded speed, to construct ideal nonlinear Hamiltonians for state preparation and logical gates, and compare it with the photon-optimal path. We find that the two paths nearly coincide for state preparation but differ markedly for logical operations, namely the brachistochrone preserves the encoded qubit during a bit flip, whereas the photon-optimal path flips a known state through the vacuum. We then introduce the tangential capacity to quantify how effectively gate sets track these paths. Using this analysis, we find that conditional squeezing achieves the highest capacity, preparing GKP states in 824 ns with a fidelity of 0.99 and a minimum closeness to the path of 0.90, compared with 0.98 and 0.51 for conditional displacements and 0.83 and 0.19 for SNAP gates.
tldr: The paper derives time- and photon-optimal control paths for preparing Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states and implementing logical bit flips, comparing nonlinear Hamiltonians and gate capabilities under photon loss.
motivation: GKP states are promising bosonic error-correcting codes but are difficult to control because they are highly non-Gaussian and sensitive to photon loss.
method: The authors use brachistochrone and photon-optimal paths to construct ideal nonlinear Hamiltonians, then introduce tangential capacity to quantify how well practical gate sets track these paths.
result: Conditional squeezing achieves the best performance, preparing GKP states in 824 ns with 0.99 fidelity and 0.90 path closeness, outperforming conditional displacements and SNAP gates.
conclusion: The analysis identifies conditional squeezing as a strong candidate for fast, high-fidelity GKP state preparation and logical operations, while highlighting the distinction between time-optimal and photon-optimal control.

title: Towards Distributed Quantum Computing: Quantum Gate Teleportation Via Satellite-Distributed Entanglement Under Atmospheric Depolarization
authors: Artur Czerwinski, Jakub J. Borkowski, Maciej Wi\'sniewski, Saeed Haddadi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate quantum gate teleportation as a primitive for satellite-enabled distributed quantum computing. In the considered architecture, a satellite distributes entangled photon pairs to two optical ground stations, which transfer the shared quantum resource to remote quantum processing units. This entanglement is then used to implement a nonlocal controlled-NOT gate between two circuit qubits located in different processors. We formulate the minimal four-qubit protocol, consisting of two network qubits that provide the entangled resource and two circuit qubits on which the distributed gate is performed. Atmospheric propagation effects in the gravitational field are modeled through an effective two-qubit depolarizing channel whose parameters depend on atmospheric and optical quantities, including the Fried parameter and receiver aperture. The performance of the protocol is quantified by the fidelity between the ideal CNOT output state and the state produced by noisy quantum gate teleportation. Our results show that the fidelity is governed by the quality of the distributed entanglement and depends jointly on atmospheric coherence, aperture size, and effective depolarization strength. These findings connect physical-layer modeling of satellite optical channels with gate-level performance in distributed quantum computing.

title: Probing Krylov Dynamics In Driven Many-Body Systems
authors: Adolfo Del Campo Andr\'as Grabarits
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Krylov complexity has become a central probe of operator growth, scrambling, and quantum chaos. Yet, a basic fact hinders its experimental study: laboratory quantum systems are routinely driven in time, whereas the Krylov construction assumes a fixed generator and breaks down once the Hamiltonian varies. Here, we solve the time-dependent many-body Krylov problem exactly and in closed form for scale- and rotation-invariant systems realized in current quantum-simulation and control platforms. We find exact relations that map the driven dynamics onto mutually orthogonal Krylov subspaces and yield a closed-form spread complexity, determined solely by the spectral properties of the initial Hamiltonian and the driving schedule. The construction extends to Liouville space and solves the time-dependent density-matrix Krylov problem, which makes the Krylov dynamics of initial thermal states experimentally accessible. In scale-invariant quantum gases, such as the driven Lieb-Liniger model, the Tonks-Girardeau gas, and the Calogero-Sutherland model, the complexity is set by the width of the atomic cloud and its rate of change, directly accessible via in situ and time-of-flight imaging. In rotation-invariant spin systems such as the Haldane-Shastry and central-spin models, it is governed by collective spin precession that can be probed and read out in trapped-ion, cavity-QED, and circuit-QED platforms.

motivation: Krylov complexity is a central probe of operator growth, scrambling, and quantum chaos, but its standard construction assumes a fixed Hamiltonian and thus fails for time-driven systems common in experiments.
method: The authors formulate and solve the time-dependent many-body Krylov problem in closed form for scale- and rotation-invariant systems, extending the construction to Liouville space and density matrices.
result: They obtain exact relations mapping driven dynamics onto orthogonal Krylov subspaces and derive closed-form spread complexity determined by initial spectral properties and the driving schedule, with explicit expressions for Lieb-Liniger, Tonks-Girardeau, Calogero-Sutherland, Haldane-Shastry, and central-spin models.
conclusion: The work makes Krylov dynamics experimentally accessible in driven quantum gases and spin systems via in situ imaging, time-of-flight, and collective spin readout, bridging quantum chaos diagnostics with realistic quantum-simulation platforms.

title: Faithful Filtering Of Constrained Quantum Records: Local Limits And Collective Advantage From Loops
authors: Qingtian Miao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weak probes can record whether neighboring spins are aligned without revealing their common orientation. Reading the probes can then herald a projection of an unknown spin state onto the aligned subspace that preserves every coherence within it. We ask how often this projection succeeds when the probes are read separately or jointly. For binary pure product records and zero false positives, we derive the exact optimum over all separable measurements, and hence over all local operations and classical communication. It is the probability that one-sided local witnesses exclude every alternative, and simultaneous local measurements attain it. Joint readout can do better by accepting coherent combinations of ambiguous outcomes in which the alternatives cancel. For pairwise parity records on a connected simple graph, it beats every local strategy exactly when the graph has a loop, at all record overlaps strictly between zero and one. For general binary linear records, the condition is an irreducible dependency among at least three records. The advantage lowers the leading power of the efficiency at weak recording. On a triangle the efficiency becomes linear rather than quadratic in the witness probability, and a three-pulse coherent-light receiver captures this gain with a single click. Extensions treat targets spanning several patterns and a noisy comparison at a common output fidelity.
tldr: The paper analyzes when weak-probe records can faithfully herald projection onto an aligned spin subspace, deriving optimal local versus collective readout strategies.
motivation: Weak probes can record relational information about spins without revealing their orientation, enabling coherence-preserving filtering of unknown states. The key question is how often such filtering succeeds under local versus joint readout.
method: For binary pure product records with zero false positives, the author derives the exact optimum over separable measurements and LOCC, then studies collective readout advantages for parity records on graphs and general binary linear records.
result: Simultaneous local measurements attain the local optimum, while joint readout can outperform all local strategies when parity records lie on a graph with a loop or when at least three records have an irreducible dependency, improving the weak-recording efficiency exponent.
conclusion: Collective coherent readout provides a genuine advantage for faithful filtering of constrained quantum records, with graph-theoretic conditions characterizing when this advantage appears.

They show that this optimum equals the probability that one-sided local witnesses exclude every alternative, and that simultaneous local measurements attain it. They then explore when joint readout can outperform local strategies by accepting coherent combinations of ambiguous outcomes in which the alternatives cancel. The advantage lowers the leading power of the efficiency at weak recording; on a triangle the efficiency becomes linear rather than quadratic in the witness probability, and a three-pulse coherent-light receiver captures this gain with a single click. Extensions treat targets spanning several patterns and a noisy comparison at a common output fidelity.

title: Local Enhancement Of Finite-strength Code Preparation: Recoverability And Wilson Coherence
authors: Tong Xu, Yuanchen Zhao, Dong E. Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stabilizer measurements provide a direct route to preparing quantum error-correcting codes and long-range entangled states. In realistic implementations, however, finite measurement strength can coherently deform the encoding map away from the projective limit. Certain nonlocal signatures associated with long-range order can survive such a deformation, but this alone does not guarantee that the resulting state protects encoded quantum information. We show that, at fixed strength, local logical leakage obstructs asymptotically faithful recovery; along logical operators' supports, its accumulation forces the relevant measurement strength to grow logarithmically with code distance. We then prove that this obstruction can be removed locally: for fixed toric registers under sufficiently weak local-stochastic errors, enhancing only a vanishing fraction of checks near selected logical supports restores recovery while the bulk remains at finite measurement strength. With recoverability restored, we prove a further dimensional distinction in logical operations. In the strict three-dimensional deconfined phase, suitable enhanced tubes restore the equivalence of macroscopically separated representatives, so either representative asymptotically implements the same controlled logical action on a fixed encoding. In two dimensions, recoverability alone does not restore this equivalence: the representatives can remain inequivalent even when both associated encodings are recoverable.
tldr: The paper analyzes finite-strength stabilizer measurements for preparing topological codes, showing local logical leakage obstructs faithful recovery but can be removed by enhancing a vanishing fraction of checks near logical supports.
motivation: Stabilizer measurements can prepare quantum error-correcting codes and long-range entangled states, but finite measurement strength coherently deforms the encoding and may undermine protection of encoded information.
method: The authors study recoverability of finite-strength code preparation, bound accumulation of local logical leakage along logical operator supports, and propose local enhancement of checks near selected logical supports in toric registers under weak local-stochastic errors.
result: They prove that, at fixed strength, local logical leakage obstructs asymptotically faithful recovery and forces measurement strength to grow logarithmically with code distance; local enhancement restores recovery while the bulk remains at finite strength, and in 3D deconfined phases enhanced tubes restore equivalence of macroscopically separated logical representatives, unlike in 2D.
conclusion: Local enhancement can overcome finite-strength recovery obstructions in topological code preparation, but logical-operation equivalence exhibits a dimensional distinction between 3D and 2D settings.

They model finite-strength stabilizer measurements as coherent deformations of the encoding map and analyze the resulting logical leakage using tools from operator algebra and recovery channel theory. For the local enhancement protocol, they use percolation theory and cluster expansion methods to show that enhancing a vanishing fraction of checks suffices to restore recovery while keeping the bulk at finite strength. title: Circuit-aware Protection Against Burst Errors In Lattice Surgery
authors: Jaebum Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale quantum computing will require logical operations protected against high-energy impacts that disturb many superconducting qubits at once. Gap engineering suppresses relaxation induced by these impacts, but protecting only a subset of qubits requires choosing where that protection is placed. During lattice surgery, measurements change as patches merge and split, exposing different ancillas and temporal boundaries to burst errors. Here we compare three static protection layouts for a simulated lattice-surgery CNOT, matching the numbers of protected ancillas and the X:Z check-type splits. At distance 9, protecting the check type measured during each merge reduces burst-induced excess risk by [MATH] relative to a deep geometric band under correlated background matching, without giving the decoder the impact parameters. We attribute this difference to report errors at temporal boundaries and ancilla faults propagating to data, which interact to increase the excess risk of a shallow band. We also find that the typed layout reaches the shallow-band reference risk with an estimated [MATH] fewer protected ancillas. At distance 13, the advantage is not resolved under oracle decoding, and a five-round burst cap reverses the shallow-band ordering. These results indicate how the measurements of a logical circuit can guide protection placement within the simulated decoder and burst-duration regimes tested here.
tldr: The paper compares static protection layouts for a simulated lattice-surgery CNOT to mitigate burst errors by placing protection according to the check type measured during each merge.
motivation: Large-scale superconducting quantum computers must withstand high-energy impacts that corrupt many qubits simultaneously, and lattice surgery dynamically changes which ancillas and temporal boundaries are exposed.
method: The author simulates a lattice-surgery CNOT at distances 9 and 13 and compares three static gap-engineering protection layouts with matched protected-ancilla counts and X:Z check-type splits under correlated burst-error models.
result: At distance 9, protecting the check type measured during each merge reduces burst-induced excess risk relative to a deep geometric band, and achieves shallow-band reference risk with fewer protected ancillas; at distance 13 the advantage is unresolved under oracle decoding and can reverse with a five-round burst cap.
conclusion: Circuit-aware placement of protection can improve burst-error resilience in lattice surgery within the tested decoder and burst-duration regimes, but the benefit depends on distance and decoding assumptions.

The layouts are: (1) a 'typed' layout that protects the check type measured during each merge, (2) a 'deep geometric band' that protects a contiguous region, and (3) a 'shallow band' reference. Using a decoder that is not given the impact parameters, they find that at distance 9 the typed layout reduces burst-induced excess risk by 38^{+6}_{-5}% relative to the deep band under correlated background matching. At distance 13, the advantage is not resolved under oracle decoding, and a five-round burst cap reverses the shallow-band ordering. title: Optical Trapping Of Neutral Atoms Via Magnetic-dipole Transitions
authors: E. Orellana-Paillaleo, N. Vera, P. Solano
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical trapping of neutral atoms is almost universally described as an electric-dipole (E1) effect. We show that the magnetic field of light, acting on a magnetic-dipole (M1) transition, can induce an ac Zeeman shift significantly larger than the ac Stark shift, thereby enabling magnetic trapping. We construct the M1 polarizability tensor and identify a critical detuning [MATH], independent of optical power, below which the magnetic interaction dominates. We analyze suitable trapping parameters and possible loss mechanisms, particularly for the intraconfigurational transitions [MATH] of erbium at [MATH]~nm and [MATH] of dysprosium at [MATH]~nm. We propose two trapping configurations: a hybrid magnetic/electric optical tweezer and an optical lattice with separated magnetic and electric antinodes, producing state-dependent purely magnetic and purely electric trapping wells. Our results present optical magnetic fields as a suitable resource to expand the toolbox for atomic manipulation.
tldr: The paper shows that magnetic-dipole (M1) transitions can produce ac Zeeman shifts large enough to optically trap neutral atoms, enabling purely magnetic or hybrid magnetic/electric trapping schemes.
motivation: Optical trapping of neutral atoms is conventionally treated as an electric-dipole effect, but magnetic-dipole transitions may offer an additional and potentially dominant trapping mechanism for suitable atomic species.
method: The authors construct the M1 polarizability tensor, identify a power-independent critical detuning where magnetic interaction dominates, and analyze trapping parameters and loss mechanisms for erbium and dysprosium transitions.
result: They propose a hybrid magnetic/electric optical tweezer and an optical lattice with separated magnetic and electric antinodes, yielding state-dependent purely magnetic and purely electric trapping wells.
conclusion: Optical magnetic fields can serve as a useful resource for atomic manipulation and expand the toolbox for neutral-atom trapping and state-dependent control.

title: Quantum Css Codes: Decoder-aware Multiobjective Design And Bound-certified Selection
authors: Jiapei Zhuang, Yaocheng Chen, Xingyao Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes trade decoding reliability against the resources needed to measure their checks. We formulate Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code design at fixed encoding resources as a decoder-aware multiobjective problem. The objectives are failure probability under sector-wise degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding and check weight, the minimum total weight of an independent pure-type generator basis. For independent bit- and phase-flip noise with perfect syndrome extraction, deterministic truncation bounds support selection under a failure-rate constraint. At a per-sector error probability of 0.01, the bounds certify that a code encoding two logical qubits into 40 physical qubits meets a failure-rate target of 0.001 at check weight 139. The lower bound of every cheaper candidate in the corresponding (40,2) main menu exceeds this target. In paired searches sharing one annealing kernel and equal query budgets, decoder-aware guidance gives significantly higher mean final hypervolume than distance guidance in all eight tested configurations under the reported Holm correction. Against distance-multiplicity guidance, five configurations show significant gains and three do not, including one with a negative mean difference. All arms are scored in common truncated-reliability and normalized-check-weight coordinates. The framework connects reliability-check-weight trade-offs to bound-certified selection within evaluated CSS pools.
tldr: The paper formulates decoder-aware multiobjective design and bound-certified selection for quantum CSS codes under fixed encoding resources.
motivation: Quantum error-correcting codes must balance decoding reliability against the resource cost of measuring checks, motivating a design framework that explicitly accounts for decoder performance and check weight.
method: The authors treat CSS code design as a multiobjective optimization problem with objectives given by failure probability under sector-wise degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding and minimum pure-type generator-basis check weight, using deterministic truncation bounds for certified selection.
result: At per-sector error probability 0.01, the bounds certify that a (40,2) code meets a 0.001 failure-rate target at check weight 139, and decoder-aware guidance outperforms distance guidance in all eight tested annealing configurations.
conclusion: The framework connects reliability-check-weight trade-offs to bound-certified selection within evaluated CSS code pools, providing a practical methodology for decoder-aware quantum code design.

title: Dissipaton-embedded Quantum Master Equation For Nonlinear System-bath Coupling

abstract: ArXiv:2611.15198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dissipaton theory was proposed more than a decade ago as a statistical quasiparticle theory for open quantum systems and was soon extended to nonlinear system-bath coupling. title: Controlled Preparation And Unconditional Transport On A Fluctuating Quantum Graph
authors: Xianbin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lieb--Robinson bounds limit the spread of quantum information, but do not establish that a prescribed input can be prepared and transmitted with appreciable probability. For quantum graphs with fluctuating edges, connecting spectral propagation to unconditional readout also requires control of graph coherence, finite boundaries, and preparation errors. We address this problem in a one-probe model on a prescribed square candidate lattice, combining a generalized Rokhsar--Kivelson parent, spectral reduction, adiabatic preparation, and local dynamical estimates. Assuming a supplied coherent graph ground state, we construct a finite-source wave packet and a hopping ramp that populate an isolated branch with strictly positive group velocity. We prove an unconditional arrival probability of at least [MATH] in a specified receiver region of a sufficiently large finite open square. Explicit bounds on local joint-state and Hamiltonian errors retain a lower probability of [MATH], without requiring global many-body state closeness or postselection on graph measurements. Exact arithmetic certificates and a separate small-system numerical diagnostic support the quantitative analysis. The construction provides a model-specific benchmark for transport and readout in fluctuating quantum networks, linking a propagation mechanism to an observable lower bound and identifying the local error budgets required to preserve it. It distinguishes suppression of unwanted influence from guaranteed signal delivery, a useful separation for quantum-network and emergent-geometry models. The resource estimates are conservative, graph-state supply is assumed, and the result does not establish background-free geometry or gravitational dynamics.

title: Squeezed Light Generation By Cooper Pair Recombination In A Superconductor-Semiconductor Structure
authors: Sima Buchbinder, Avi Koriat, Alex Hayat
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theoretically demonstrate squeezed light generation in a compact, electrically driven device utilizing the nonlinear light-matter interaction of Cooper-pair recombination in a hybrid superconductorsemiconductor structure. On the basis of second-order perturbation theory, we developed an effective Hamiltonian which incorporates the electronic component of the interaction as a photon coupling strength coefficient, enabling a model to describe the quadrature squeezing effect of Cooper-pair recombination on the photonic state. We find the squeezing strength to be proportional to the superconducting energy gap squared and device length, as well as increasing with applied voltage. For practical device length, materials and voltage bias, we calculated squeezing values comparable to those of existing squeezed light generation methods when operating below the critical temperature. This theoretically developed concept shows viability for electrically pumped squeezed light generation and can pave the way towards realization of squeezing in compact integrated structures.

title: Reducing Tls Losses In Superconducting Circuits Using Solid Neon
authors: A. Palmer, K. Matkovic, P. Russell, E. Helgemo, L. Delventhal, Y. Ashlea Alava, K. Zuo, S. N. Coppersmith, M. C. Cassidy
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two level systems (TLSs) are a major source of loss in superconducting devices, limiting the performance of qubits, detectors, and resonators. These defects arise from a range of sources, including surface oxides, crystal defects, as well as fabrication residues which are often difficult to remove. Using NbTiN coplanar waveguide resonators, we show that depositing and subsequently removing a solid neon film can significantly improve device performance. Analysis of the temperature and power dependence indicates that this enhancement arises from reduced TLS dissipation, which we attribute to the redistribution and removal of surface contaminants during neon deposition and evaporation. Atomic force microscopy images of contaminated hexagonal boron nitride flakes before and after neon exposure show that neon treatment can redistribute and remove surface residues. These results demonstrate a simple, non-destructive approach for mitigating TLS losses in superconducting devices and other sensitive materials that cannot withstand aggressive cleaning processes.

title: High-precision Measurement Of Level Leakage Via Intelligent Coherent Control
authors: Ting Wang, Hang Xu, Shi-Qiang Qiao, Xue-Ke Song, Haipeng Cao, Zhao-Feng Su, Liu Ye, Dong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Level leakage constitutes a dominant error source in quantum state control and necessitates accurate characterization for large-scale quantum computing. Quantum sensing provides a viable route for high-precision estimation of level leakage, but its sensitivity can be limited by non-unitary leakage dynamics and interference between the free Hamiltonian and signal generator. This work proposes a reinforcement learning-based quantum sensing algorithm for Hermitian three-level and effective dissipative two-level systems. The algorithm adopts an experimentally feasible pulse-parameter modulation strategy, enabling high-precision and reliable measurement under the specified control and measurement protocol. In both models, DQN-discovered pulse sequences enhance the measurement-model-specific sensing precision, while joint phase--detuning modulation further improves the performance and yields a CFI close to the corresponding QFI.

title: An Architecture For Real-Time Quantum Error Correction With Neutral Atoms
authors: X. Wang, Y. Jing, Z. Yu, S. Wang, D. Niu, Y. Liu, T. Xiao, A. Yang, J. Han, Y. Wu, X. Lv
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The latency of quantum measurement and classical decoding constrains the execution of adaptive fault-tolerant circuits. In neutral-atom processors, this requirement couples spatially resolved fluorescence detection to classical inference. title: Quantum Synchronization In Xx Chains Under Relaxation

abstract: ArXiv:2611.14657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study stable synchronization in qubit XX chains with site-dependent frequencies and exchange couplings under multi-local amplitude damping noise, extending the uniform-chain results of B. akmak et al., [Phys. Rev. A 114, L030202 2026] in several directions. We establish that the dark-mode energies are precisely the eigenvalues shared by all undamped segments separated by the damped sites. Generic stable synchronization of the edge qubits occurs if and only if these segments share exactly one eigenvalue and this eigenvalue is nonzero, in which case every qubit on the support of the corresponding dark mode is synchronized with locking constants independent of the initial preparation. This spectral matching condition identifies the Hamiltonian parameters that support synchronization, while the couplings to the damped sites control the relative oscillation amplitudes. We present analytical examples which show how inhomogeneity can create synchronization absent in uniform chains and turn preparation-dependent locking into generic synchronization. We also calculate the asymptotic pairwise concurrence and prove that, in the single-dark-mode regime, every pair participating in synchronized oscillations remains entangled with a nonzero, constant concurrence.

title: Evaluating Quantum Circuit Protection Methods After Compilation: An Empirical Comparison
authors: Ing Muyleang, Leanghok Hour, Youngsun Han
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum cloud providers can read the circuits they receive and their outputs, yet methods for hiding a circuit are usually evaluated on the circuit as written, before compilation optimises it. We compare three ObfusQate schemes (inverse, composite and delayed gates), ECQCO and Q-MaskCut under one protocol that compiles every protected circuit at optimisation level 3 before measuring it; the goal is to keep the provider from learning the user's algorithm and answer. Q-MaskCut is one example combination of existing techniques: a one-time-pad key, decoy wires, circuit cutting with a random rotation pair across each cut, and Pauli twirling with dynamical-decoupling masking after compilation. We simulate 11 circuits of 3 to 19 qubits without noise and on two noise models, measure the compiled structure and execution time of 23 circuits of 3 to 127 qubits, and test whether the structural disguise survives a second compilation by the provider. Composite and delayed gates lose most of their structural disguise in compilation and leave the output readable; inverse gates keep a high normalised graph edit distance (normGED) only by making execution 7 to 112 times longer; ECQCO's output could not be decoded with the implementation provided by its authors. Q-MaskCut hides the output (mean total variation distance without the key 0.94), and without noise, with exact fragment probabilities, it decodes exactly. Its compiled normGED of 0.88 comes mostly from the masking, which a second compilation removes, leaving 0.42 from the key, decoys and padlocks. With noise, its fidelity is comparable to the original's; it needs 7 to 91 fragment variants per circuit in the simulations (7 to 61 in a run on ibm_marrakesh) and a classical reconstruction. Protection should therefore be evaluated on the compiled circuit and again after the provider recompiles it.
tldr: The paper empirically compares quantum circuit protection/obfuscation schemes after compilation and shows that most structural disguises fail under compilation or provider recompilation.
motivation: Quantum cloud providers can read submitted circuits and outputs, so users may want to hide their algorithms, but existing obfuscation methods are typically evaluated before compilation optimizes the circuit.
method: The authors compile every protected circuit at optimization level 3 and compare three ObfusQate schemes, ECQCO, and Q-MaskCut using structural metrics, execution time, noise simulations, and recompilation tests.
result: Composite and delayed gates lose their disguise, inverse gates remain structurally different only at large execution-time cost, ECQCO could not be decoded with the provided implementation, and Q-MaskCut hides outputs but its structural masking is largely removed by recompilation.
conclusion: Circuit protection should be evaluated on the compiled circuit and again after provider recompilation, and Q-MaskCut requires further work to survive recompilation and practical fragment overhead.

title: A New Framework For Quantum Reinforcement Learning
authors: Mohsen Heidari Alireza Tavakoli
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) has emerged as a promising approach for controlling quantum systems and accelerating learning tasks with quantum resources. However, most existing QRL formulations still retain a classical reinforcement learning interface: states and actions are often encoded in computational bases and rewards are extracted through measurements. This interface is restrictive for genuinely quantum environments: choosing a measurement can discard entanglement information, while repeated intermediate measurements collapse the evolving state and require costly re-preparation. This motivates a fully QRL framework in which the agent, environment, rewards, and return accumulation are all quantum. In this paper, we take a step toward this goal and introduce a new QRL framework in which both the policy and the environment are modeled by conditional quantum channels. We then propose a quantum policy-gradient algorithm for parameterized conditional quantum channels with a trainable control basis. We also derive finite- and infinite-horizon gradient estimators using a new parameter-shift rule. This rule is needed because policy parameters are shared across repeated interaction blocks and the infinite-horizon objective is not a finite circuit; rather than shifting every occurrence and evaluating the whole trajectory, our estimator shifts only one sampled policy block. Sampling this block from a geometric distribution yields an unbiased gradient estimator under bounded rewards. Finally, we establish convergence of the resulting stochastic gradient-ascent procedure to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size assumptions.
tldr: The paper proposes a fully quantum reinforcement learning framework using conditional quantum channels for both policy and environment, with a quantum policy-gradient algorithm and new parameter-shift gradient estimators.
motivation: Existing quantum reinforcement learning formulations often keep a classical interface via computational-basis states, actions, and measurement-based rewards, which discards entanglement and causes state collapse. The authors aim for a fully quantum agent-environment-reward-return framework.
method: They model policy and environment as conditional quantum channels, introduce a trainable control basis, and derive finite- and infinite-horizon gradient estimators using a parameter-shift rule that shifts only one sampled policy block drawn from a geometric distribution.
result: The proposed estimator is unbiased under bounded rewards, and the stochastic gradient-ascent procedure is shown to converge to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size assumptions.
conclusion: This work takes a step toward fully quantum reinforcement learning by providing a channel-based policy-gradient framework with convergence guarantees, though it remains a quantum machine learning/control contribution rather than an information-theoretic one.

title: From Optimization To Construction: Expanding Quantum Measurement Designs
authors: Taotao Zhao, Qianjun Yao, Mengdi Sun, He Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating molecular energies on quantum computers requires repeated measurements of many Pauli terms, making sampling a major resource cost. Measurement design chooses which compatible terms are measured together and allocates a finite shot budget among bases to minimize the variance of an energy estimator. We introduce variance-guided measurement group construction (VGMC), which reduces variance beyond optimization on existing measurement bases by changing which Hamiltonian terms share measurement shots. After including every Hamiltonian term measurable in each existing basis, we jointly optimize estimator coefficients and shot allocations to separate inefficient use of these measurements from limitations of their measurement combinations. We compare a candidate's benefit with the cost of withdrawing shots from existing bases, and use the resulting scores to guide greedy construction of qubit-wise commuting groups followed by joint re-optimization. With exact covariances, VGMC outperformed the state-of-the-art measurement design methods across the molecular benchmarks where it introduced additional measurement bases, achieving variance reductions of 18.19%-23.38%. The gains persisted with approximate covariances, and simulations with finite shots indicated lower estimated shot requirements near chemical accuracy. These results show that optimizing how measurements are combined can also guide which terms are measured together, offering a route to reducing the sampling overhead of variational quantum simulation while retaining local measurements on current and near-term devices.
tldr: VGMC improves quantum measurement design for molecular energy estimation by constructing new qubit-wise commuting measurement groups and jointly optimizing shot allocation and estimator coefficients.
motivation: Estimating molecular energies on quantum computers requires many Pauli measurements, so reducing measurement and sampling overhead is a key practical challenge for variational quantum simulation.
method: The authors introduce variance-guided measurement group construction, which adds all measurable Hamiltonian terms to existing bases, jointly re-optimizes coefficients and shots, and greedily constructs qubit-wise commuting groups using scores that balance variance reduction against shot withdrawal costs.
result: With exact covariances, VGMC reduced variance by 18.19%–23.38% over state-of-the-art measurement design methods on molecular benchmarks where it introduced new bases, and gains persisted with approximate covariances and finite-shot simulations.
conclusion: Optimizing how measurements are combined can guide which Hamiltonian terms should be measured together, offering a practical route to lower sampling overhead in near-term variational quantum simulation while retaining local measurements.

title: QSim-Arena: An Evolving Developer For Quantum Simulation Advantage
authors: Jue Xu, Yue Wang, Qi Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Where practical advantage emerges in quantum dynamics simulation remains a central debate in quantum computing. Claimed advantages can be rapidly narrowed or overturned by stronger classical methods, while progress on both sides can outpace the journal publication cycle. We present QSim-Arena, a research framework in which AI agents combine a closed loop of verification and benchmarking with open exploration. Hamiltonians, initial states and accuracy targets for evolved states or observable expectation values provide explicit specifications for evaluating simulation methods. Agents translate published techniques into executable components, reproduce reported results and benchmark their performance across diverse Hamiltonian families. Competing classical methods are implemented and independently crosschecked, providing credible baselines for end-to-end quantum resource estimates based on rigorous error bounds and empirical calibration. Alongside this closed loop, agents recombine classical simulation techniques and co-design fault-tolerant quantum circuits using knowledge extracted from the literature. Initial applications improve baseline resource estimates through the integration of established techniques. QSim-Arena thus treats quantum advantage assessment as an evolving, reproducible research process that can respond to advances in algorithms, error analysis and hardware.
tldr: QSim-Arena is an AI-agent-driven research framework that continuously verifies, benchmarks, and co-designs classical and fault-tolerant quantum methods for quantum dynamics simulation to assess where practical quantum advantage actually exists.
motivation: Claims of quantum simulation advantage are fragile — they can be overturned by improved classical algorithms faster than the journal cycle, so a reproducible, evolving evaluation process is needed.
method: AI agents translate published simulation techniques into executable components, reproduce reported results, benchmark them across Hamiltonian families against independently implemented classical baselines, and recombine techniques to co-design fault-tolerant circuits with resource estimates.
result: Initial applications integrate established techniques to improve baseline end-to-end quantum resource estimates based on rigorous error bounds and empirical calibration.
conclusion: The authors frame quantum advantage assessment as an ongoing, reproducible research process that adapts to advances in algorithms, error analysis, and hardware.

title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks With Nisq Modules Inside A 30-Billion-Parameter Llm
authors: Maforikan Amoussou, Borja Aizpurua, Sukhbinder Singh, Rom\'an Or\'us, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's [MATH] hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into [MATH] disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an [MATH]-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with [MATH] trainable parameters ([MATH], [MATH], [MATH], [MATH]) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing [MATH] of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within [MATH]-[MATH] of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a [MATH]-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.
tldr: The authors replace contiguous spans of transformer blocks in a 30B-parameter LLM with multi-head quantum neural network modules built from angle-encoded NISQ circuits plus classical mixers, trained by statevector simulation and run on an IBM Heron processor.
motivation: Encoding thousands of hidden neurons into a qubit register is impractical, so the paper seeks a NISQ-compatible quantum module that can substitute for transformer blocks at production scale with far fewer parameters.
method: The hidden space is partitioned into disjoint heads, each angle-encoded into a small qubit register, processed in parallel by parameterized entangling circuits with learned readouts, and coupled by constrained classical linear layers (mixers); checkpoints are trained classically via exact statevector simulation and the quantum heads executed on hardware.
result: A single multi-head QNN with roughly a few thousand trainable parameters replaces eight transformer blocks in Qwen3-30B-A3B, but controls with the entangler switched off, frozen angles, or random angles beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical MLP remains a few percent ahead.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in and executed within a production-scale LLM, but provides no evidence of a genuine quantum advantage over classical or disentangled controls.

title: One Molecule, Many Outputs; Many Molecules, One Output: Exact Diagnostics For Atom-level Compositional Quantum Encoders
authors: Ashwanth Krishnan Gautami Sanjay Naik
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15092v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum natural language processing (QNLP) turns the grammar of a sentence into a tensor network and then into a quantum circuit with trainable angles. We build such a model for molecules: each heavy atom is a word with one wire per bond, and each bond is a ``cup'' joining two wires, so the circuit's wiring is the molecular graph. We work out exactly what these circuits keep. With the typed angle sharing of lambeq, the circuits separate every isomer pair we tested. Yet for isomers that simpler sharing confuses, the output states stay almost the same, before and after training. On 7 Tox21 pairs and 1,988 MOSES pairs, nearly all the difference lies in how often the measurements succeed, which a standard readout ignores. Simpler sharing, by element and bond type, shows why: the output then depends only on a graph whose vertices are the bonds. This explains all but one of the identical-output pairs we certify, including 1.19\% of 232{,}191 MOSES molecules, and for alkyl side chains it reduces to a tree shape that tells chains apart up to 15 atoms but not from 16. On small pairs, this circuit and the 1-WL graph test each separate pairs the other misses. We also show that SMILES writing order can change the output, that a run succeeds with probability at most [MATH] for [MATH] bonds, and that a cup-free design avoids this cost. No circuit beats a simple atom-count model on Tox21, and we claim no quantum advantage.
tldr: This paper constructs QNLP-style quantum circuits from molecular graphs and gives exact diagnostics of what graph information their output states and measurement probabilities retain.
motivation: The authors aim to understand whether compositional quantum encoders based on grammar-derived tensor networks can distinguish molecular isomers and what structural information such circuits preserve after training.
method: Heavy atoms are encoded as words and bonds as cups in a lambeq-style tensor-network-to-quantum-circuit construction; the authors analyze output states, measurement success probabilities, and graph-invariant limitations for Tox21 and MOSES molecular pairs.
result: Typed angle sharing separates tested isomer pairs, but many differences appear only in measurement success probabilities ignored by standard readout; simpler sharing reduces outputs to bond-graph features, and no circuit outperforms a simple atom-count baseline on Tox21.
conclusion: The work provides exact diagnostics and cautions against overinterpreting QNLP molecular encoders, explicitly claiming no quantum advantage and showing that graph-structural limitations dominate the observed behavior.

title: A Field-Deployable 2u Ultra-Stable Laser With Sub-Hertz Linewidth Based On Optoelectronic Oscillator Locking
authors: Dongdong Jiao, Linbo Zhang, Xue Deng, Jing Gao, Yue Gao, Mengfan Wu, Qi Zang, Guanjun Xu, Tao Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compact, high-performance ultra-stable lasers that can operate outside the laboratory remain a long-standing goal. Here we report, to our knowledge, the most compact field-deployable ultra-stable laser, packaged in a standard 2U rack chassis. It is stabilized to a 50 mm-long, 19 mL optical reference cavity with low vibration sensitivity by optoelectronic oscillator (OEO) locking, an approach particularly suited to compact, transportable systems. The laser delivers an integrated linewidth of about 0.42 Hz and a fractional frequency stability of about 5E-15 at 1 s averaging time (about 2.2E-15 at 0.4 s). Measured phase noise approaches the cavity thermal-noise limit below 100 Hz and the theoretical OEO-locking limit from 100 Hz to 100 kHz. The system volume is roughly one quarter of the volume of previously reported integrated, transportable ultra-stable lasers of comparable performance, making it well suited for field applications in time-frequency metrology, quantum technologies, and environmental sensing.
tldr: The authors demonstrate a 2U rack-mounted, field-deployable ultra-stable laser with 0.42 Hz integrated linewidth and 5E-15 fractional frequency stability at 1 s, stabilized via optoelectronic-oscillator locking to a 50 mm optical cavity.
motivation: Compact, transportable ultra-stable lasers with sub-Hertz linewidths are needed outside the laboratory for time-frequency metrology and quantum technology applications, but existing transportable systems are bulky.
method: A 50 mm-long, 19 mL low-vibration-sensitivity optical reference cavity is locked using an optoelectronic oscillator (OEO) locking scheme chosen for its suitability to compact systems, with the whole apparatus packaged in a standard 2U rack chassis.
result: The system achieves ~0.42 Hz integrated linewidth, ~5E-15 stability at 1 s (2.2E-15 at 0.4 s), phase noise approaching the cavity thermal-noise limit below 100 Hz, and roughly one quarter the volume of comparable integrated transportable ultra-stable lasers.
conclusion: The laser offers laboratory-grade frequency stability in a field-deployable package, targeting applications in time-frequency metrology, quantum technologies, and environmental sensing.

title: Quantum Recurrent Architectures For Financial Time Series Prediction
authors: Danyal Maheshwari, Gerhard Hellstern, Martin Zaefferer, Martin Braun, Tanja D\"ohler
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study evaluates quantum classical hybrid recurrent architectures for financial time-series forecasting: a Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) network and Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) with lag-based inputs. Classical lag vectors are encoded into quantum states via amplitude encoding, which compactly represents normalized observations but requires nontrivial state preparation; the QLSTM gates and the QRC reservoir are implemented with parameterized quantum circuits, while classical optimizers train the interface and readout layers. On a monthly revenue series extended to 1056 months by a Gaussian-process--hidden-Markov generator, with a fixed chronological 70/15/15 split and one-step-ahead forecasts, we compare both models against a full-size LSTM, a classical control matched in parameter budget and interface architecture, a small plain LSTM, and classical reservoir computing, over ten seeds and against persistence, seasonal-naive and SARIMA benchmark forecasts. The QLSTM, with 2,105 parameters, is statistically indistinguishable from an LSTM 126 times larger, but equally indistinguishable from the matched classical control and from a plain LSTM of the same budget, so its parameter efficiency cannot be attributed to the quantum circuits. The quantum reservoir is worse than a classical reservoir of equal feature dimension in all ten seeds and worse than SARIMA, whereas all recurrent models and both classical reservoirs improve on SARIMA by about 2\% in RMSE. In a 24-month rolling-origin backtest the classical LSTMs degrade more slowly than the QLSTM. We find no evidence of a quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage in this low-dimensional setting.
tldr: Benchmarks a quantum LSTM and quantum reservoir computing against classical baselines on a low-dimensional financial revenue series and finds no quantum advantage.
motivation: Quantum recurrent architectures are often claimed to offer parameter efficiency and accuracy gains; the authors test whether such claims hold for small, low-dimensional financial time series.
method: Classical lag vectors are amplitude-encoded into parameterized quantum circuits implementing QLSTM gates and a quantum reservoir, trained with classical optimizers and compared against matched classical LSTMs, classical reservoir computing, persistence, seasonal-naive and SARIMA baselines over ten seeds and a rolling-origin backtest.
result: The QLSTM is statistically indistinguishable from a 126x larger LSTM but also indistinguishable from a parameter-matched classical control and a same-budget plain LSTM; the quantum reservoir underperforms a classical reservoir in all ten seeds and loses to SARIMA.
conclusion: No evidence of quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage exists in this low-dimensional setting, so the observed performance cannot be attributed to the quantum circuits.

title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Optimization For Cvrptw: A Systems Framework With Provable Feasibility And Empirical Hardware Limits
authors: Syamasundar Gopasana, Swatantra Singh, Rohan Joydhar, Shubhashis Sengupta
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solving large-scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems with Time Windows (CVRPTW) remains challenging because strict operational constraints and scale limit both exact and heuristic methods. We present a hybrid classical-quantum architecture combining Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) with vehicle-level Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), solved using Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald quantum processors. The decomposition avoids the variable growth and constraint-enforcement difficulties of monolithic CVRPTW QUBO formulations. We evaluate the framework on five realistic benchmarks derived from London traffic and location data, spanning 10--70 customers, using a validation pipeline enforcing feasibility and monotone improvement over classical baselines. SQBM+ achieves verified fleet-distance reductions of 2.80% (7,927 m) for the 25-customer instance and 0.22% (1,186 m) for the 55-customer instance. QAOA experiments establish a current hardware boundary for reliable constraint satisfaction at subproblems of up to 4 customers (16 qubits). Diagnostic results identify assignment-level time-window tightness, rather than local route optimization, as the dominant scalability bottleneck. The results demonstrate a practical near-term role for hybrid classical-quantum optimization while establishing empirical limits for current quantum hardware.
tldr: This paper presents a hybrid classical-quantum systems framework for solving the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW) using MILP decomposition and vehicle-level QUBO solved with Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on current quantum processors.
motivation: Large-scale CVRPTW instances are difficult for exact and heuristic classical methods due to strict constraints and scale, motivating near-term hybrid quantum-classical optimization approaches.
method: The authors decompose CVRPTW into a MILP master problem and vehicle-level QUBO subproblems, solved with Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald hardware, with a validation pipeline enforcing feasibility and monotone improvement over classical baselines.
result: SQBM+ achieves verified fleet-distance reductions of 2.80% for a 25-customer instance and 0.22% for a 55-customer instance, while QAOA reliably satisfies constraints only up to 4-customer subproblems (16 qubits), identifying assignment-level time-window tightness as the dominant scalability bottleneck.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical near-term role for hybrid classical-quantum optimization but establishes empirical hardware limits for reliable constraint satisfaction on current quantum devices.

title: Sensing Frequencies At The Discrete Grover-Heisenberg Limit Using A Single Qubit
authors: Boyang Chen, Andrea Coladangelo, Jerry Li, Haocheng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a fundamental quantum sensing task: detecting weak oscillating fields with unknown strength and frequency. Recent work by Allen et al. established a fundamental lower bound on the required sensing time, which they named the "Grover-Heisenberg limit", and gave a protocol attaining this limit. The protocol relies on auxiliary qubits, which are used to run Grover's algorithm as a subroutine, leaving open the question of whether a single sensing qubit can achieve the same scaling. We show that a single qubit suffices for a discrete version of this problem, in which the signal strength is known and the frequency belongs to an arbitrary, but known, finite set of candidate frequencies. Our protocol's sensing time grows only as the square root of the number of candidate frequencies. We prove that this square-root dependence, which we refer to as the "discrete Grover-Heisenberg limit", is optimal in the worst case.
tldr: The paper shows a single sensing qubit can achieve a discrete Grover-Heisenberg-limited scaling for frequency discrimination among a known finite set of candidate frequencies.
motivation: Prior work established a Grover-Heisenberg limit for sensing weak oscillating fields but required auxiliary qubits to run Grover search; this work asks whether a single qubit can attain the same scaling.
method: The authors design a single-qubit sensing protocol for the discrete problem where the signal strength is known and the frequency belongs to a known finite set, and they prove a worst-case optimality bound on the sensing time.
result: The protocol's sensing time scales as the square root of the number of candidate frequencies, and the authors prove this square-root dependence is optimal in the worst case.
conclusion: A single qubit suffices for discrete Grover-Heisenberg-limited frequency sensing, resolving an auxiliary-qubit requirement in this restricted setting.

title: Scalable Compilation Of Resource-Efficient Tapers For High-Confidence Quantum Phase Estimation
authors: David Raveh, Andrew Sornborger, Yi\u{g}it Suba\c{s}\i, Lukasz Cincio
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15076v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum phase estimation is a key component of many quantum algorithms. Recently, high-confidence, tapered QPE (tQPE) has been introduced, significantly reducing the number of ancilla qubits necessary for a given failure probability, [MATH]. We consider tQPE with [MATH] ancillas, where [MATH] represents the number of ancillas necessary to estimate a phase to a given resolution and [MATH] represents the number of ''confidence'' qubits added to ensure a desired success probability. With tQPE the failure probability decays double exponentially in [MATH], implying that only a few confidence qubits suffice for virtually any problem of interest. A key challenge for tQPE is the construction of the quantum circuit for preparing the taper state on the ancilla register. Here, we develop scalable tensor network methods (previous work was limited to ([MATH])) giving highly optimized state preparation circuits for optimally concentrated DPSS (Slepian) tapers. We provide an accompanying database of resource-efficient state preparation circuits for [MATH] and [MATH]. Our circuits are shallow enough for a demonstration on near-term devices for small values of [MATH]. We run tQPE circuits for a 1-qubit system initialized in the ground state on Quantinuum's H2-2 quantum computer, demonstrating a [MATH] to [MATH] reduction in failure probability for [MATH] on a noisy device.
tldr: The paper develops scalable tensor-network compilation of resource-efficient taper-state preparation circuits for high-confidence tapered quantum phase estimation and demonstrates the circuits on a near-term trapped-ion device.
motivation: High-confidence tapered QPE can drastically reduce the number of ancilla qubits needed for a target failure probability, but constructing the required taper-state preparation circuit for larger ancilla registers is a key practical bottleneck.
method: The authors use tensor-network methods to optimize shallow state-preparation circuits for optimally concentrated DPSS/Slepian tapers, provide a database of circuits for selected ancilla sizes and taper widths, and run tQPE experiments on Quantinuum's H2-2 quantum computer.
result: They obtain resource-efficient taper-state preparation circuits that are shallow enough for near-term demonstration and observe a substantial reduction in failure probability on a noisy device for a one-qubit ground-state phase estimation instance.
conclusion: The work makes tQPE more experimentally accessible by automating the compilation of taper-state preparation circuits, though its focus is quantum-algorithm compilation and hardware demonstration rather than the researcher's listed information-theoretic or thermodynamic directions.

title: Cumulants Of Operator Semigroups For Hierarchies Of Many-Particle Evolution Equations
authors: V. I. Gerasimenko
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper presents a brief overview of recent advances in the mathematical theory of evolution equations for quantum many-particle systems. The structure of expansions representing non-perturbative solutions to the Cauchy problem for hierarchies of fundamental evolution equations for many quantum particles is outlined. It has been shown that the concept of cumulants of operator semigroups forms the basis for non-perturbative representation of solutions to hierarchies of evolution equations that describe the state and observables. It is proven that the constructed dynamics of correlations underlie the description of the evolution of the state, both for finitely and infinitely many particles, governed by the BBGKY hierarchy for reduced density operators or by the hierarchy of nonlinear evolution equations for reduced correlation operators. In fact, it is demonstrated that the behavior of particle correlations governs the dynamics of states in quantum systems with an infinite number of particles.
tldr: The paper reviews non-perturbative solution methods for hierarchies of evolution equations in quantum many-particle systems using cumulants of operator semigroups.
motivation: To provide a mathematical framework for describing the dynamics of correlations and states in quantum systems with finitely or infinitely many particles governed by BBGKY-type hierarchies.
method: It employs cumulant expansions of operator semigroups to construct non-perturbative representations of solutions to the Cauchy problem for hierarchies of evolution equations for reduced density operators and correlation operators.
result: The paper shows that the constructed correlation dynamics underlie state evolution in both finite and infinite quantum particle systems, and that particle correlations govern the dynamics of states.
conclusion: Cumulants of operator semigroups provide a general mathematical basis for non-perturbative analysis of many-particle quantum evolution hierarchies, emphasizing the role of correlations in infinite-particle systems.

title: On The Statistical Reliability Of Chaotic Simulations At Reduced Precision
authors: Peter V. Coveney Ross Ah-Weng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.15344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, while AI workloads are driving its growing prominence in hardware design. Yet small arithmetic errors do not necessarily imply accurate statistics. Finite representation limits spatial resolution, while rounding can merge trajectories that should separate in chaotic systems, progressively concentrating probability on a shrinking collection of computer states. This redistribution can distort statistical averages well before periodicity becomes apparent; furthermore, disjoint computational basins can induce an initialisation bias, even when the intended equilibrium statistics are independent of the initial ensemble. We use functional graphs and their transfer operators to connect these pathologies to bounds on statistical bias, the duration of accurate averaging, and the effect of reducing precision. Exhaustive numerical experiments on four chaotic maps, with 1-24 significand bits and the 24-bit endpoint matching IEEE FP32, show how initially accurate ensembles drift towards incorrect statistics, with lower precision often bringing this deterioration forward. Stochastic rounding substantially extends some useful averaging windows but leaves others severely biased. Longer computed trajectories can therefore worsen inferred statistics, and a finite average can outperform the "infinite-time" computer average by orders of magnitude.
